Well, I'm here because... well, it's been going on for a year now. A whole year of just... digging, trying to get to the bottom of it. See, I'm a phlebotomist, so I know how these things work, I know what I'm looking at when I see a lab report. And for the past year, I've been trying to prove that someone—I don't know exactly who yet, but someone in the clinic system—is changing or, or holding back parts of my dad's lab results. 

I mean, I saw the original numbers. I know what I saw. But then, when I look at his chart now, it just doesn't match. It doesn't make any sense. And I've talked to his doctors, I've brought the printouts, I've highlighted the discrepancies, and they just... they brush me off. They tell me the numbers are fine, that everything is normal. Even my family—my sister, my mom—they just sigh and tell me to let it go, that the doctors know best. But they don't see what I see. They don't understand that someone is deliberately altering his medical records. 

It's just... it's exhausting. I spend hours every night going over the portals, cross-referencing everything, trying to find the exact point where the data was manipulated. And no matter how many people tell me I'm wrong, I know I'm right. I know what I saw. But fighting this... fighting the whole system, and my family... it's just really wearing me down. I can't sleep, I can't focus at work because I'm just constantly thinking about who is doing this to him and why.

Well, harm? I mean... that's the million-dollar question, isn't it? Why would someone do this? Are they trying to hide a mistake? Are they experimenting with his treatment? Are they just... I don't know, malicious? I don't know if they're holding back the real numbers to directly hurt him, like physically, or if it's some sort of cover-up, but the effect is the same, isn't it? If his doctors aren't getting the right data, how can they treat him properly? 

And that's what I keep telling my mom and my sister. I say, "Look, if his potassium was actually 3.2 on the 14th, but the portal says 4.1 on the 15th, and there's no record of a supplement being given, where did that jump come from?" I know how these systems interface. I know how the LIS communicates with the EMR. You don't just get a spontaneous correction without an audit trail. But when I ask for the audit trail, suddenly I'm the crazy one. Suddenly I'm being "unreasonable." 

So, yes, I think the act of changing his records is inherently harmful. Whether they are sitting in some office laughing about it and twirling a mustache... probably not. But someone is making a conscious decision to alter or withhold his lab results. I saw the original printout from the reference lab. I held it in my hand. And what's in his chart right now is a lie. And no matter how many times Dr. Evans or Dr. Miller pat my hand and tell me the numbers are fine, they aren't looking at the real numbers! They're looking at the manipulated data. And it's just... it's destroying me, trying to get someone, anyone, to just look at the proof I have.

Misinterpreted? No, no, absolutely not. See, that’s exactly what Dr. Miller tried to tell me last month. Another explanation? Like... like what, exactly? A computer glitch? A typo that magically corrects itself across three different screens? A cosmic ray hitting the server room? I mean, believe me, I have racked my brain trying to find another explanation. Because, honestly? It would be so much easier if it were just a system error. It would be a relief. 

But I’ve spent the entire last year—a full 365 days of waking up every single morning with this horrible, heavy knot in my stomach—trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. I've looked at it from every angle. I know how the laboratory information systems work. If an analyzer misreads a sample and a tech has to go in and manually verify or correct a value, there is a flag. There is an asterisk, a footnote, a digital footprint that says 'amended report.' But there is nothing here. Just a clean, seamless set of numbers that completely contradicts the physical printout I held in my own hand.

And I just... I keep hitting this brick wall. No matter how many doctors sit me down—Dr. Miller, Dr. Evans, the specialists—and no matter how many times my own family members, my mom and my sister, look at me with pity and tell me the numbers are fine, that I need to let it go... I can't. I can't let it go because I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw. I know it in my bones. 

And having to fight this battle every single day, having to be the only one who cares enough to stand up and say 'wait, this isn't right, look at the discrepancy'... it’s wearing me down. It is wearing me down to a point where I can barely sleep. I can barely focus on my own patients at work because I'm constantly re-running my dad's panels in my head, trying to figure out who is doing this and why. If there was another, innocent explanation, why wouldn't they just show me the audit logs when I asked? Why hide behind closed doors and treat me like I'm a nuisance? So, no. No, I don't think there's another explanation. I really don't.

It would be a relief. \n\nBut I’ve spent the entire last year—a full 365 days of waking up every single morning with this horrible, heavy knot in my stomach—trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. My memory? You... you think I just misremembered? No. No, absolutely not. I mean, think about what you're actually asking me. You're asking if my brain just magically conjured up a completely different set of metabolic values out of thin air? 

Look, I know I keep repeating myself, I know I probably sound like a broken record to you, but I'm here because for the past year—this entire, exhausting, miserable year—I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. I didn't just forget. I have a highly trained memory for this specific kind of data. It's my livelihood! When I looked at his initial printout, I burned those numbers into my brain because it’s my dad, you know? It’s not just some random patient file in a stack of a hundred. I stared at that paper. I traced the columns with my own finger. I noted the exact highs and lows. 

So to have everyone... I mean, no matter how many doctors, or my mom, or my sister, just pat me on the shoulder and tell me the numbers are fine, or that my memory is playing tricks on me because I'm stressed out... it’s incredibly insulting. It feels like everyone is trying to gaslight me. I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw. I know it with absolute, one-hundred-percent certainty. And having to constantly defend my own brain, my own memory, to every single person I talk to... it’s wearing me down. I am just so unbelievably worn down by having to justify my own sanity when I know exactly what was on that page.
